title: Top Local Payment Methods in the Philippines: How Filipinos Pay
summary: From GCash and QR Ph to bank transfers and 7-Eleven, see how Filipinos pay online and in store, and how to accept every method with one integration.
body_markdown:
Filipinos now make most retail payments digitally, and the methods they use are changing fast. In 2025, QR Ph passed card transactions for the first time, e-wallets carried 41% of online spending, and cash on delivery still accounted for 23% of e-commerce value. The payment methods you offer at checkout decide which of these customers can complete a purchase. This guide covers the seven payment method categories that matter most in the Philippines, who uses each one, and the mix to start with for your business. Each section links to a deeper guide.


**Key takeaways**


- Digital payments reached 64.7% of retail transaction volume in 2025, up from 20.1% in 2020, according to the BSP.


- E-wallets lead online at 41% of e-commerce value. Offer GCash and Maya first.


- QR Ph processed 2.47 billion transactions in 2025 and passed card transactions for the first time.


- Cash on delivery still made up 23% of e-commerce value. OTC payments collect that cash before you ship.


- Cards, bank transfers, direct debit and BNPL cover high-value, recurring, cross-border and installment purchases.


- Xendit supports 100+ payment methods plus cards in the Philippines on a single integration.


## **How Filipinos pay today**


The Philippines has crossed a milestone: most retail payments are now digital. Digital payments made up


[64.7%](https://www.philstar.com/business/2026/08/18/2549941/digital-payments-now-make-647-philippines-retail-transactions) of retail transaction volume in 2025, up from 57.4% in 2024 and just 20.1% in 2020, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP).


Online, e-wallets lead by a wide margin. Digital wallets accounted for


[41% of e-commerce value in 2025](https://fintechnews.sg/128337/e-commerce/southeast-asia-payment-methods-2026-global-payments-report/) , while bank-to-bank (account-to-account) payments reached 13%.


Cash has not gone away, though. The same report found that cash on delivery still made up 23% of e-commerce value, and cash was 42% of in-store spending, the highest share of any market in the study. A good Philippine checkout serves both groups: the wallet-first majority and the customers who still prefer to pay in cash.


This guide walks through the seven payment method categories that matter most, who uses each one, and when to offer it. Each section links to our in-depth guide for that category.

The options listed are those Xendit supports in the Philippines today; the market has more providers in each category.


## **1. E-wallets: the default for Filipino shoppers**


E-wallets are the single most important payment method in Philippine e-commerce, with 41% of online value in 2025. They are used for everything from online shopping and bills to sending money home, and many users hold a wallet account even without a traditional bank account.


The wallets that matter most:


- GCash: the country’s largest e-wallet, connecting more than 94 million users to over 6 million merchants (same source).


- Maya: the other major e-wallet, with a strong base among urban shoppers and small businesses.


- GrabPay: tied to the Grab ecosystem of rides, food delivery and rewards.


- ShopeePay: the go-to wallet for Shopee shoppers and promo-driven online purchases.


How it works: the customer picks a wallet at checkout, is redirected to the app, and confirms with an MPIN or OTP. Payment is confirmed instantly.


When to offer it: always, if you sell to consumers. With Xendit, you can accept GCash, Maya, GrabPay and ShopeePay, with limits up to PHP 100,000 per transaction. GCash (through GCash Link and Pay), Maya, GrabPay and ShopeePay can also be linked once for recurring and one-click payments.


***Read also:***[E-Wallets in the Philippines: A Business Guide to Accepting GCash, Maya, and More](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/e-wallets-in-the-philippines-a-business-guide-to-accepting-gcash-maya-and-more/)


## **2. QR Ph: one code for every bank and wallet**


QR Ph is the Philippines’ national QR standard, set by the BSP and running on the InstaPay real-time network. One code accepts payment from any participating bank or e-wallet, so customers of GCash, Maya, BPI, BDO, UnionBank and others can all pay the same merchant.


It is now bigger than cards. QR Ph processed 2.47 billion transactions worth PHP 1.16 trillion in 2025, overtaking debit and credit card transactions for the first time. On Xendit, QR Ph was the


[second most used payment method in the Philippines in 2025](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/qr-ph-payments-in-the-philippines-a-business-guide-to-the-countrys-national-qr-standard/) , at 17% of transactions.


How it works: the merchant shows a QR Ph code at the counter, on a checkout page or in a payment link. The customer scans it with any participating app, checks the merchant name and amount, and approves.


When to offer it: for physical stores, sari-sari and F&B businesses, events, and online checkouts where customers prefer to pay from their bank app. It is also a quick way to collect on invoices through payment links. With Xendit, QR Ph supports payments from PHP 1 to PHP 50,000.


***Read more:***[QR Ph Payments in the Philippines: A Business Guide to the Country's National QR Standard](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/qr-ph-payments-in-the-philippines-a-business-guide-to-the-countrys-national-qr-standard/)


## **3. Over-the-counter (OTC) payments: cash, without cash on delivery**


With cash on delivery still at


[23% of e-commerce value](https://fintechnews.sg/128337/e-commerce/southeast-asia-payment-methods-2026-global-payments-report/) , many Filipino shoppers still want to pay in cash. Over-the-counter payments let them do that at a convenience store, pawnshop or payment centre near home, while the merchant gets paid before shipping, with none of the failed-delivery risk of COD.


The Philippines has one of the densest OTC networks in the region, including 7-Eleven, pawnshop chains such as Cebuana Lhuillier, M Lhuillier and Palawan Express, courier LBC, mall bills-payment counters at SM and Robinsons, and ECPay’s network of partner outlets.


How it works: the customer receives a payment reference at checkout, goes to any partner outlet, and pays the cashier. The merchant is notified once the payment is posted.


When to offer it: for customers without bank accounts or e-wallets, first-time online buyers, customers outside Metro Manila, and categories like gaming, education and online lending repayments. Xendit supports 12 OTC channels, with limits up to PHP 200,000 on some channels.


## **4. Bank transfer via InstaPay and PESONet: trusted for bigger payments**


Bank transfers in the Philippines run on two BSP rails: InstaPay for real-time transfers and PESONet for batch, higher-value transfers. Both are growing fast; in 2025, PESONet transactions overtook cheque payments for the


[first time](https://tribune.net.ph/2026/08/19/bsp-digital-payments-account-for-nearly-two-thirds-of-retail-volume) .


For online checkout, the standard is a virtual account: a unique account number assigned to each customer or order. Each payment lands against its own number, so it is matched to the right order automatically, with no proof-of-payment screenshots to check.


How it works: the customer receives an account number at checkout and pays it through any banking or e-wallet app on InstaPay or PESONet, internet banking, or an ATM. The merchant receives confirmation once the transfer arrives.


When to offer it: for higher-value purchases, B2B invoices, tuition, insurance premiums and real estate payments. With Xendit, bank transfer payments go up to PHP 200 million per transaction.


***Read also:***[Bank Transfer Payments in the Philippines: Everything Your Business Needs to Know About InstaPay and PESONet](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/bank-transfer-payments-in-the-philippines-everything-your-business-needs-to-know-about-instapay-and-pesonet/)


## **5. Direct debit: link once, pay again**


Direct debit lets a customer link their bank account to your business and approve payments directly in their bank app, without typing card or account details each time. Some direct debit products also let the merchant charge the account on a schedule once the customer has agreed.


How it works: the customer chooses their bank at checkout, logs in to authorise the link, and approves the payment. For recurring products, later charges run automatically.


When to offer it: for subscriptions, insurance premiums, loan repayments and marketplaces with frequent repeat buyers. With Xendit, you can accept BPI, UnionBank and RCBC direct debit, with BPI Recurring and UnionBank eADA supporting merchant-initiated, recurring charges.


***Read more:***[Direct Debit in the Philippines: A Guide for Businesses Managing Recurring Payments](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/direct-debit-in-the-philippines-a-guide-for-businesses-managing-recurring-payments/)


## **6. Credit and debit cards: essential for high-value and international buyers**


Cards now trail QR Ph in transaction count (


[Philstar, citing BSP](https://www.philstar.com/business/2026/08/18/2549941/digital-payments-now-make-647-philippines-retail-transactions) ), but they remain essential for higher-value online purchases, subscriptions, travel, and customers paying from abroad. Card acceptance also matters for Filipinos who want to earn rewards or pay over time with their bank’s instalment programme.


How it works: the customer enters card details at checkout and usually completes a 3D Secure check with their bank. Cards can be saved for one-click and recurring billing.


When to offer it: for SaaS and subscriptions, travel and hospitality, premium retail, and any business with foreign customers. With Xendit, you can accept Visa, Mastercard and JCB in PHP or USD, charge saved cards for recurring payments, and take Apple Pay on payment links. Xendit was the first payment provider to offer Apple Pay in the Philippines.


***Read also:***[Credit Card Payments in the Philippines: A Complete Guide for Growing Businesses](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/credit-card-payments-in-the-philippines-a-complete-guide-for-growing-businesses/)


## **7. Buy now, pay later (BNPL): instalments without a credit card**


Many Filipinos who shop online do not have a credit card. BNPL fills that gap by letting approved customers split a purchase into instalments, which is especially useful for gadgets, appliances, fashion, and education.


How it works: the customer chooses a BNPL provider at checkout, is approved, and picks an instalment plan. The provider pays the merchant and carries the credit risk.


When to offer it: for larger baskets where a lump-sum payment might stop the sale, and for younger shoppers without credit cards. With Xendit, you can offer BillEase, with purchases up to PHP 150,000.


***Read more:***[Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) in the Philippines: A Complete Guide for Businesses](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/buy-now-pay-later-bnpl-in-the-philippines-a-complete-guide-for-businesses/)


## **How to choose the right payment mix**


There is no single best method; the right mix depends on what you sell, your average order value, and how many of your customers are unbanked. As a baseline, GCash and Maya, plus QR Ph, reach most digital payers, and OTC captures shoppers who still want to pay in cash.

A few practical rules help whichever mix you choose. Show GCash and Maya first on mobile. Offer at least one cash option if many of your customers are outside Metro Manila or new to online shopping. Track success and drop-off rates per method, then add or reorder options based on what your own customers use.

## **Frequently asked questions (FAQ)**


**What is the most popular payment method in the Philippines?**


Online, it is e-wallets, led by GCash and Maya, at 41% of e-commerce value in 2025. In person, cash is still the single largest method, but QR Ph is growing fast and overtook cards in transaction count in 2025.


**Is cash on delivery still necessary?**


COD still made up 23% of online payment value in 2025. Offering OTC payments at 7-Eleven, pawnshops, and bill-payment centres lets cash-preferring customers pay upfront, which removes the failed-delivery and cash-handling risks of COD.


**What is the difference between InstaPay and PESONet?**


InstaPay is the real-time rail for smaller transfers and powers QR Ph. PESONet handles batch transfers with higher limits, which makes it a better fit for large B2B and supplier payments.


**Which methods support recurring payments?**


Cards, linked e-wallets (GCash Link and Pay, Maya, GrabPay and ShopeePay) and recurring direct debit (BPI Recurring and UnionBank eADA) can all be charged again after the customer’s first authorisation.


**Can I accept payments from customers without a bank account?**


Yes. E-wallets and OTC payments both work for unbanked customers, and together they cover most Filipinos who do not hold a traditional bank account.
